제 3 부 보 증 강 조｝'
I.

어휘 보충 Test
이 부분에서는 고시 • 대기업공채 출제 경향에 대비하여 강세 • 발음 • 철자 등 어휘 자체의 지식
을 묻는 문제를 우측에 수록했고, 좌측에는 그에 대한 본 자료를 정리하여 좌우 대칭이 되도록
하였다. （학습자는 별도의 해설이 없어도 자기판정을 할 수 있다） 필요한 이에게는 상당히 요긴
한 자료가 될 것이다.
반의어의 출제빈도는 그리 높지 않지만, 대학교양 수준의 400문제를 엄선하여 수록해 놓았다.
GRE에 대비하는 학습자는 집증적으로 학습할 수 있다.

II.

영작문 Test
총 20회의 분량에 각각 객관식 5문항과 주관식 5문항을 수록했다.
객관식의 경우, 문법과 어법을 묻는 문제가 대종을 이루나, 주관식의 경우 생활영어 표현으로부
터 기사 영작문에 이르기까지 다양한 문체가 출제된다. 주관식의 모범답안 외에도 달리 표현할
수 있는 방법이 많으므로 가능한 한 다양한 표현을 시도해 보는 것이 효과적이다.

1.

실전 Test
실전 Test는 본강의 종합문제가 5지선다형인 것과는 달리 4지 선다형으로 구성되어 있다.
실전에 임하는 기분으로 시간을 재어 가며 풀어볼 것이며, 정오 분석을 통해 취약점이 발견되면
본강의 해당부분을 집중 학습하여 보완하기 바란다.

2. 聽 사전의 참고
본강 학습에 흥미를 느끼는 학습자를 위하여 다음의 두 사전을 추천한다.
• Longman Dictionary of Contemporary English <New Edition>
• Col 1 ins CobuiId English Language Dictionary <1987>

3. 진도표의 활용
GRADUATE ENGLISH에는 진도표가 삽입되어 있다.

책 전체를 구분하여 학습일정（날짜와 시간）을 기록해 두고 계획성있는 면학을 하기를 권한다. 특히 본
인의 필요에 의해 선별학습을 할 경우 진도표는 매우 유익할 것이다. 1 차학습시 못다한 부분을 2 차 -3 차
학습을 통해 보충하도록 한다. 진도표는 개인학습은 물론 강의참여時나 공동학습 （ Group Study） 時에도 활용
할 수 있다.
부지런한 자만이 앞으로 나아갈 수 있고 높이 오를 수 있다. 이 책으로 공부하는 많은 학생들이 끈기를
가지고 진도표의 모든 공간을 검게 메꾸기를 기대한다.

trapped in the poverty cycle gradually lessened as

My fellow citizens：
Today, we celebrate the mystery of American
renewal.
This ceremony is held in the depth of winter.
But, by the words we speak and the faces we show
the world, we force the spring. -- a spring reborn
in the world’s oldest democracy, that brings forth
the vision and courage to reinvent America.
When our founders boldly declared America’s
independence to the world and our purposes to the
Almighty, they knew that America, to endure, would
have to change. Not change for change’s sake, but
change to preserve America’s ideals -- life,
liberty, the pursuit of happiness. Though we march
to the music of our time, our mission is timeless.
Each generation of Americans must define what it
means to be an American.
*
On behalf of our nation, I salute my predecessor
President Bush for his half-century of service to
America, and I thank the mill ions of men and women
whose steadfastness and sacrifice triumphed over
depression, fascism, and communism.
Today, a generation raised in the shadows of the
Cold War assumes new responsibilities in a world
warmed by the sunshine of freedom but threatened
sti11 by ancient hatreds and new plagygg Raised in
unrivaled prosperity, we inherit an economy that is
stil1 the world’s strongest, but is weakened by
business failures, stagn^t wages, increasing
inequality, and deep divisiuhs among our own
people.
When George Washington ijrst took the oath I
have just sworn to uphohifF추Jews traveled slowly
across the land by horseback and across the oceans
by boat. Now, the sights and sounds of this
ceremony are broadcast i ns tantaneously to billions
around the world. Communications and commerce are
global； investment is mobile； technology is almost
magical； and ambition for a better life is now
universal. We earn our 1ivelihood in America today
in peaceful competition with people all across the
earth. Profound and powerful forces are shaking and
remaking our world, and the urgent question of our
time is whether we can make change our friend and
not our enemy.
This new world has already enriched the lives of
millions of Americans who are able to compete and
win in it. But when most people are working harder
for less； when others cannot work at all: when the
cost of heal th care devastates families and
threatens to bankrupt our enterprises, great and

We know we have to face hard truths and take

confidence. Though our challenges are fearsome, so

To renew America we must be bold.
We must do what no generation has had to do
before. We must invest more in our own people and
their jobs, and in their future, and at the same

It will not be easy； it will require sacrifice.
But it can be done, and done fairly, not choosing

We must provide for our nation the way a family

Our founders saw themselves in the light of

Chimps and children, gulls and Greeks -- the 아hgjpkists go their merry way, comparing bi安 of human
cultural behavior with bits of genetically programmed animal behavior. True, humans are animals； they
share certain ^natom|cal ^jea^ures with other animals, and some items of human behavior may seem
analogous to the behavi3rof other animals. But such analogies can seriously mislead if we fail to look
at the context of a particular item of behavior. Thus one ethologist compares the presentation of aCgWig
by a cormorant with ^£ft-giving in humans. Yet the cormorant’s twig-presentation simply inhibits attack
and is comparable to other agpe^sement rituals found in many species. Human gift-giving differs in form
and purpose not only from culture to culture, but within the same culture in various social contexts.
Everything significant about it derives from its social context. Thus, ethologists can accomplish little
-- beyond reminding us that we are animals -- until they study humans as cultural beings.

“I have considered the structure of al 1 volant
animals, and find the folding continuity of the
bat’s wings most easily accommodated to the human
form. Upon this model I shall begin my task
tomorrow, and in a year expect to tower into the
air beyond the malice or pursuit of man. But I will
work only on this condition, that the art shall not
be divulged, and that you shall not require me to
make wings for any but ourselves."
“Why,” said Rasselas, “should you envy others so
great an advantage? All ski 11 ought to be exerted
for universal good； every man has owed much to
others, and ought to repay the kindness that he has
received. ”
“If men were all virtuous,” returned the artist,
“I should with great alacrity teach them all to
fly. But what would be the security of the good, if
the bad could at pleasure invade them from the sky?
Against an army sailing through the clouds neither
wall, nor mountains, nor seas, could afford any
security. A flight of northern savages might hover
in the wind, and light at once with irresistible
violence upon the capital of a fruitful region that
was rolling under them. Even this valley, the
retreat of princes, the abode of happiness, might
be violated by the sudden descent of some of the
naked nations that swarm on the coast of the
southern sea. ”

Inaugural

Address

W코lliam J.

Cl i n 1.01-1,

It is time to break the bad habit of expecting
something for nothing, from our government or from
each other. Let us all take more responsibility,
not only for ourselves and our families but for our
communities and our country.
To renew America, we must revitalize our
democracy.
This beautiful capital, I ike every capital since
the dawn of civilization, is often a place of
intrigue and calculation. Powerful people maneuver
for position and worry endlessly about who is in
and who is out, who is up and who is down,
forgetting those people whose toil and sweat sends
us here and pays our way.
Americans deserve better. And in this city
today, there are people who want to do better. And
so I say to all of you here, let us resolve to
reform our politics, so that power and privilege no
longer shout down the voice of the people. Let us
put aside personal advantage so that we can feel
the pain and see the promise of America.
Let us resolve to make our government a place
for what Frankl in Roosevelt called “bold,
persistent experimentation,” a government for our
tomorrows, not our yesterdays.
Let us give this capital back to the people to
whom it belongs.
To renew America, we must meet challenges abroad
as well as at home. There is no longer a clear
division between what is foreign and what is
domestic. The world economy, the world environment,
the world AIDS crisis, the world arms race -- they
affect us all.
Today, as an old order passes, the new world is
more free but less stable. Communism’s collapse has
called forth old animosities and new dangers.
Clearly America must continue to lead the world. We
did so much to make.
While America rebuiIds at home, we will not
shrink from the challenges, nor fail to seize the
opportunities, of this new world. Together with our
friends and allies, we will work to shape change,
lest it engulf us.
When our vital interests are chailenged, or the
will and conscience of the international community
is defied, we wil1 act -- with peaceful diplomacy
whenever possible, with' force when necessary. The
brave Americans serving our nation today in the
Persian Gulf, in Somalia, and wherever else they
stand are testament to our resolve.
But our greatest strength is the power of our
ideas, which are still new in many lands. Across
the world, we see them embraced -- and we rejoice.

[Cont inued from page 120]
42nd President of the U. S. A.

Our hopes, our hearts, our hands, are with those on
every continent who are building democracy and
freedom. Their cause is America’s cause.
The American people have summoned the change we
celebrate today. You have raised your voices in an
unmistakable chorus. You have cast your votes in
historic numbers. And you have changed the face of
the Congress, the presidency, and the political
process itself.
Yes, you, my fellow Americans, have forced the
spring. Now, we must do the work the season demands.
To that work I now turn, with all the authority
of my office. I ask the Congress to join with me.
But no President, no Congress, no government can
undertake this mission alone.
My fellow Americans, you, too, must play your
part in our renewal.
I challenge a new generation of young Americans
to a season of service -- to act on your idealism
by helping troubled children, keeping company with
those in need, reconnecting our torn communities.
There is so much to be done -- enough indeed for
millions of others who are sti11 young in spirit to
give of themselves in service, too.
In serving, we recognize a simple but powerful
truth： We need each other. And we must care for one
another.
Today, we do more than celebrate America； we
rededicate ourselves to the very idea of America：
-- An idea born in revolution and renewed
through two centuries of chailenge；
- - An idea tempered by the knowledge that, but
for fate, we -- the fortunate and the unfortunate
-- might have been each other；
- - An idea ennobled by the faith that our nation
can summon from its diversity the deepest measure
of unity；
- - An idea infused with the conviction that
America’s long heroic journey must go forever
upward.
And so, my fellow Americans. As we stand at the
edge of the 21st century, let us begin anew with
energy and hope, with faith and discipline, and let
us work until our work is done. The scripture says,
“And let us not be weary in well-doing, for in due
season, we shall reap, if we faint not. **
From this joyful mountain top of celebration, we
hear a call to service in the valley.
We have heard the trumpets. We have changed the
guard. And now -- each in our own way, and with
God’s help -- we must answer the call.
Thank you, and God bless you all.

colour and shape. We ignore the miracle of the
ear, which conveys images that are far deeper,
more subtle and more penetrating than the eye.

sound. Sound goes directly into our bodies. What
the aural can do to the inside of our brain, to
the “within” of our lives, nothing else can do.

alliances conducted on every continent and at

engagement between the great powers. Which is

An orator, whose purpose is to persuade men, must speak the things they wish to hear； an orator,
whose purpose is to move men, must also avoid disturbing the emotional effect by any obtrusion of
intellectual antagonism, but an author, whose purpose is to instruct men, who appeals to the intellect,
must be careless of their opinions and think only of truth. It will often be a question when a man is or
is not wise in advancing unpalatable opinions, or in preaching heresies； but it can never be a question
that a man should be si lent if unprepared to speak the truth as he conceives it. Deference to popular
opinion is one great source of bad writing and is all the more disastrous because the deference is paid
to some purely hypothetical requirement. When a man fails to see the truth of certain generally accepted
views, there is no law compelling him to provoke animosity by announcing his dissent. He may be excused
if he shrink from the lurid glory of martyrdom； he may be justified in not placing himself in a position
of singularity. He may even be commended for not helping to perplex mankind with doubts which he feels
to be founded on limited and possibly erroneous investigation. But if allegiance to truth lays no stern
command upon him to speak out his immature dissent, it does lay a stern command not to speak out
hypocritical assent. There are many justifications of silence： there can be none of insincerity.

Excusez-Moi! Speakez-Vous Franglais?

The best way to deal with a foreigner, any
old-school Brit will tel 1 you, is to shout at the
blighter in English until he catches on. If he
professes not to understand, just turn up the
volume till he does. A man who doesn’t speak
English is a man who isn’t worth speaking to.
Robert Byron, the great traveler of the ’30s who
wrote so feelingly on Islamic culture, got great
comic effect by treating every alien he met -- even
an American -- as an unintelligible buffoon； and
his John Bullish contemporary Evelyn Waugh all but
enunciated a Bl imp’s Code by asserting that no man
who knew more than one laguage could express
himself memorably in any. (Take that, Nabokov! Ft
tu, Samuel Beckett!)
To speak or not to speak： it is a question at
least as old as moody Danes delivering English
couplets. And every year, as summer approaches, we
face the same dilemma： whether to try, when in
Rome, to speak as the Romans do or to rely on
Italian cabbies speaking English (with brio, no
doubt, and sprezzatura). In some respects, it comes
down to a question of whether ’tis better to give
or to receive 1inguistic torture. The treachery of
the phrase book, as every neophyte soon discovers,
is that you cannot begin to fol low the answer to
the question you’ve pronounced so beautifully -and, worse still, your auditor now assumes you’re
fluent in Swahili. Yet sticking to English, it’s
easy to feel that you’ve never left home at all
(and are guilty, to boot, of a Waugh-like
linguistic imperialism).
In recent years of course, the spreading of the
global village has made cross-purposing a little
easier. We think it only natural to ask for hors
d’oeuvres from a maitre d’ -- as natural, perhaps,
as disucssing Realpolitik and the Zeitgeist with a
Hamburger. And as English has become a kind of
1ingua franca, all of us are fluent in Franglais
and in Japlish. It really is possible for an
un-self-made man, arriving in Paris, to ask a
mademoiselle for a rendezvous and then take her for
le fast food and le dancing and even, perhaps, le
parking. But later she may call him un jerk, and he
may get upset if he doesn’t know that the term, in
French, means an expert dancer.
The problems are most acute, in fact, when both
parties think they’re speaking the same language：
Shaw’s famous crack about England and America being
“two countries separated by the same language” is
30 times as true now that up to 60 countries claim
English as their mother — or at least stepmother
-- tongue. An Australian wil1 invite you to a
hotel, and you may be shocked if you don’t know
that it’s what you think of as a bar. An Indian
will “prepone” a meeting, and only if you’re quick
enough to calculate “postpone” in reverse have you
any chance of showing up on time. Above all, as
English has become a kind of prized commodity -and a status symbol -- in many corners of the
world, those of us born in possession of it are apt
to feel as vulnerable as a bejeweled dowager in a
dark back alleyway. There’s always someone waiting
to jump out and mug us with his English -- before

we can try out our Bahasa Indoesia on him.
And yet, and yet, there is to all this another
dimension. For in speaking a foreign language, we
tend to lose years, as well as other kinds of time,
to become gentler, more innocent, more courteous
versions of ourselves. We find ourselves reduced to
basic adjectives, like “happy” and “sad,” and
erring on the side of including our “monsieurs, ”
and we are obliged to grow resourceful and
imaginative in conveying our most complex needs and
feelings in the few terms we remember (like a child
rebuiiding Chartres out of Lego blocks). Think of
how English sounds as spoken by Marcello
Mastroianni - romantic, suggestive, helplessly
endearing. Might the same not be true in reverse?
Peter Falk appearing in a German movie (^ings of
Desire) seems almost as exotic as Isabelle Adjani
in an American one.
Speaking a foreign language, we cannot so easily
speak our minds, but we do willy-nilly speak our
hearts. We grow more direct in another tongue and
say the things we would not say at home -- as if,
you might say, we were under a foreign influence.
Inhibitions are the first thing to get lost in
translation* “je t'ainie” comes much more easily
than “I love you.” Small wonder, perhaps, that
spies are gifted 1inguists by nature as well as by
training (John le Carre was one of the most
bri1liant language students of his day)； entering
another tongue, we steal into another self.
And even when we’re not speaking Spanish but
only English that a Spaniard wil1 understand, the
effect is just as rejuvenating. How vivid the
cliche “over the hill” sounds when we’re explaining
it to an Osaka businessman! How rich the idiom
“raining cats and dogs!” Speaking English as a
second language, we find ourselves rethinking
ourselves, simplifying ourselves, committed, for
once, not to making impressive sentences but just
to making sense. English is the official language
of the European Free Trade Association, though none
of its six members has English as its mother
tongue. Why? Well, says the secretary-general
disarmingly, “using English means we don’t talk too
much, since none of us knows the nuances.”
Besides, whether we inflict our French on the
concierge or not, many of our transactions wil1
come down, in the end, to an antic game of
charades. English may be the universal language,
but it’s still less universal than hands and eyes.
So even as we become unwitting James Joyces -coining neologisms by the minute -- when we essay a
foreign language, we also become Marcel Marceaus：
asking the way to the rest room with our eyebrows
or sending back the squid with a paroxysm of mock
pain. Ask a man in Tierra del Fuego to point you to
The Sound of Music, and he’ll instantly reply, “No
problem!” (which, in very language, means that your
problems are just beginning). Then he’ll direct you
to the Julie Andrews musical that the Argentines
call The Rebel Nun. And when you say “Thank you” to
him -- in Spanish -- it can almost sond like a kind
of grace.

5 > When the Earth Cracks Open

In The spring of 1872, the naturalist John Muir was
was asleep in a small cabin in the Yosemite Valley.
“At half past two o’clock, ” he wrote later, “I was
awakened by a tremendous earthquake... the strange
thri11ing motion could not be mistaken, and I ran
out of my cabin, both glad and frightened,
shouting, ‘A noble earthquake! A noble earthquake!’
feeling sure I was going to learn something.”
It would be delightful to think that he actually
uttered those words, looking for sermons in the
shaking stones. In any case, Muir was alone in the
moonlit mountains, and so he could indulge his
charming 19th century awe. When the earth turned in
its sleep, it crushed much 1andscape in the folds,
but somehow the event could keep its innocence.
When nature does something awful, after all, is it
part of the eclectrical display of God the Father,
or merely geography rearranging itself, obeying an
impersonal agenda?
When the earth cracks open to dismantle a city,
then metaphysical questions come boiling up. What
would Muir learn? What does the cataclysm have to
teach? That the earth retains its genius for the
wild surprise? Or that some profound principle of
disorder and annihilating wrath has been set loose
in the world?
Of all natural disasters, the earthquake somehow
is the most unnerving. It is the earth talking,
after all, and so it speaks with a primal power.
Earthquakes in Scripture mean the God has crumpled
up the order of the world and hurled it down in
disgust. “And the foundations of the world do
shake,” says Isaiah. “The earth is utterly broken
down.” Or, agnostically, earthquakes are a
wandering, enigmatic fierceness, now and then
breaching the surface like Moby Dick.
An earthquake rides on a principle of
disintegration -- the disintegration not only of
architecture and pavements and lives but also of
the entire idea of order, of process and human
control. “What can one believe quite safe,” asked
Seneca, “if the world itself is shaken, and its
most solid parts totter to their fall... and the
earth lose its chief characteristic, stability?”
The familiar world goes rioting down to rubble.
Reality comes to rest at a crazy angle.
The terror lies first in the surprise. An
earthquake is hidden from one moment to the next,
as the future is hidden, as God is hidden. The
event does not announce itself as most other
disasters do, as a hurricane does, or a flood, or
even an erupting volcano, which is after all hard
to miss as dangerous geography. A plague too
arrives more slowly. That is no consolation, but at
least the mind and nerves are prepared. The event
proceeds in a logical continuum of developing bad
news.
An earthquake is simply an unannounced
convulsion. It is nature performing a Shakespearean

tragedy that begins absurdly in the fifth act：
after 15 seconds, Hamlet and the others lie dying,
the stage is covered with blood and debris. For
many years one may have lived on top of the San
Andreas fault and made doomy jokes about it； it is
like having a violent beast in the basement,
knowing that one day it may burst up through the
1iving-room floor. But there is no preparation for
the moment. Only certain animals feel premonitory
vibrations undetectable to humans. They grow
skittish. Horses glare with a wild panicked eye.
Sometimes storms, even hurricanes, can be
exhilarating. It is fun to stand on a beach during
a histrionic blow. An earthquake is not that kind
of thrill. The worst part may be the feeling of
helplessness. There is no right thing to do just
then, except perhaps to flee the building. There is
no knowing where the earth wil1 open next. The wiid
cracking follows no principle but the terrifyingly
random. Denial (“this is not happening”) competes
with fascination.
A major earthquake lays waste the human sense of
scale. When reporters write about earthquakes, they
invariably say that cars and other large objects
were “tossed around like toys.” Architecture
collapses upon itself. The human idea of proportion
is outraged in the rifting and shearing.
So certainties vanish. The earth liquefies. It
becomes as wild as surf. The solid is abruptly
fluid. Normally, earth is the refuge, the
stability, the foundation of things, The earth
should be alive only to grow vegetables and
flowers. Now the earth i tself becomes a beast, all
teeth and gashes and sudden topplings. Reality has
turned molten and violent.
Sometimes when the earth cracks open, it
produces good stories. In March 1933, Albert
Einstein was visiting the Long Beach campus of the
University of California. He and his host from the
department of geology walked through the campus,
intently discussing the motions of earthquakes.
Suddenly they looked up in puzzlement to see people
running out of campus buildings. Einstein and the
other scientist had been so busy discussing
seismology that they did not notice the earthquake
occurring under their feet.
There may be something perversely cathartic
about earthquakes. For some time mankind has been
in the business of manufacturing its own disasters
-- wars, acid rain and other pollutions, drugs, a
globe aswarm with refugees. Perhaps it is a relief
for a moment to be face to face with a disaster
that man did not invent, a cataclysm that has as
least a sort of innocence of origin in larger
powers.
The survivors wil1 proceed like Odysseus and his
men, after one of their escapes： “And so we sailed
on, aching in our hearts for the companions that we
lost, but glad to be alive.”

exchange of money for goods leaves nothing in

emotional explosions and irrational excuses, he

need help to regain the world of reality, the

stems from the class struggle that is unique to the
capitalist system -- that racial prejudice is
generate! by capitalists as a means of controlling
workers. His thesis works relatively well when
appiied to discrimination against Blacks in the
United States, but his definition of racial
prejudice as “racially-based negative prejudgments
against a group generally accepted as a race in any
given region of ethnic competition,” can be
interpreted as also including hostility toward such
ethnic groups as the Chinese in California and the
Jews in medieval Europe. However, since prejudice
against these latter peoples was not inspired by
capitalists, he has to reason that such antagonisms
were not really based on race. He disposes thusly

Prior to Newton, Aristotle had established
that the natural state of a body was a state
of rest, and that unless a force acted upon it
to maintain motion, a moving body would come
to rest. Galileo had succeeded in correctly
describing the behavior of falling objects and
in recording that no force was required to
maintain a body in motion. He noted that the
effect of force was to change motion. Huygens
recognized that a change in the direction of
motion involved acceleration, just as did a
change in speed, and further, that the action
of a force was required. Kepler deduced the
laws describing the motion of planets around
the sun. It was primarily from Galileo and
Kepler that Newton borrowed.

Human hopes are always of two kinds. A
human being has hopes for himself -- hopes
that are individual and personal. At the same
time, he has suprapersonal hopes for the human
race or for some fraction of it： his tribe,
his family, perhaps, or his church.
These two kinds of human hope are
not
always sharply distinguishable form each
other. Self-centeredness, which seems to be
one of the characteristics of life, is so
powerful a force that it invades even our
suprapersonal hopes. In fact, “nosism"(or
weism) as we may call this collective
counterpart of “egotism,” is the most
form of self-centeredness. Whether for good or
for evil, man is far stronger when he is
acting collectively than when he is playing a
lone hand； and also, when he is acting
collectively, he can behave selfishly without
being pul led up short by his conscience,
because he can delude himself into believing
that he is subordinating his self-centeredness
to the common interest, when in truth he is
merely expanding his self-conteredness to the
plural number from the singular. Thus
self-conteredness may invade our suprapersonal
hopes. On the other hand, our personal hopes
may take the form of a moral reaction against
self-centeredness and of an effort to
transcend it.

With respect to that theory of the forms of life peopling our globe, with which Darwin’s name is
bound up as closely as that of Newton with the theory of gravitation, nothing seems to be further from
the mind of the present generation than any attempt to smother it with ridicule or to crush it by
vehemence of denunciation. “The struggle for existence” and “natural selection” have become household
words and everyday conceptions. The reality and the importance of the natural processes on which Darwin
founds his deductions are no more doubted than those of growth and multiplication； and whether the full
potency attributed to them is admitted or not, no one doubts their vast far-reaching significance.
Wherever the biological sciences are studied, the “Origin of Species” lights the path of the
investigator： wherever they are taught it permeates the course of instruction. Nor has the influence of
Darwinian ideas been less profound beyond the realms of biology. The oldest of all philosophies, that of
evolution, was bound hand and foot and cast into utter darkness during the millennium of theological
scholasticism. But Darwin poured new life-blood into the ancient frame： the bonds burst, and the
revivified thought of ancient Greece has proved itself to be a more adequate expression of the universal
order of things than any of the schemes which have been accepted by the credulity and welcomed by the
superstition of weventy later generations of men.

An important development in twentieth-century literary criticism was the growth of the New Criticism.
The New Critics assumed that the methods devised for reading long poems could be applied to novels. In
practice this meant a new emphasis in the reading of fiction on scrupulous textual analysis as a
prerequisite for biographical and ideological comment. A novelist’s ideas were now significant mainly as
components of his or her writing technique. Insisting on close attention to a text,
analyzed long passages of a novel and concentrated on discerning the development of
By analyzing symbols in this way, the critic could show how the meaning of a symbol
repeated in different passages. This permitted a more complete understanding of the
than that which could be discovered through isolated symbol-hunting. One novelist who benefited from
this new emphasis on text was D. H. Lawrence, whose work was rescued from hostile critics who had
attacked it as mere ideology.

The socialization process in America has
historically been characterized by the interaction
of clearly structured, we11-organized groups that
share a sense of mission about the future of the
nation and codes of behavior wi th roots in common
principles. Americans were a diverse people, but
communities were bound by religious beliefs, ethnic
backgrounds, and strong family relationships. The
old configuration of socializing institutions no
longer functions in the same way. Mobility is one
factor in the changing picture. One fifth of all
Americans change their residences every year, but
they do not “pack” their culture. They simply move,
breaking old community ties. There is no migration,
just movement -- motion without melody.
A second factor is depersonalization. Emerson
once wrote that an institution is the lengthened
shadow of one man. Today’s insti tution is more
likely to be the lengthened shadow of itself. The
breakdown of the old configuration requires a
reconceptualization of the whole socialization
process, but the very fact of breakdown means that
fewer and fewer people even understand what is
required of a socialization process. By now the
process of social decompression may be
irreversible.

7 > How Climate Changes

Only two things are certain about the world’s
climate -- and one of them is that it will a1 ways
be unpredictable. The forces that govern i t are
preposterously intertwined, linking the chemistry
of the deep oceans to the physics of the
stratosphere, the ice-fields of the Arctic to the
forest canopies of the tropics. 11 is as difficult
to find a single cause for a climate change as it
is to pinpoint the sneeze on which to blame an
epidemic of influenza. Such complexi ty leads to the
other certainty about climate： it is in perpetual
flux.
The change that concentrates the minds of
politicians and scientists today lies in an
abundance of carbon dioxide. This colourless,
tasteless and non-toxic gas, constantly produced by
every animal around, seems an unlikely source of
worry. But it has special talents： it is a much
better trapper of heat than are the gases that make
up the bulk of the atmosphere. That much is a
certainty of molecular physics. There is no doubt
that carbon dioxide -- as vvell as several other
gases, including methane and the man-made CFCs -enhances the atmosphere’s greenhouse effect.
Because its level has been rising ever since people
took to burning wood, coal and what-have-you in
industrial quantities, the amount of heat being
trapped by it must be increasing.
This greenhouse effect is not controversial.
Nei ther is i t synonymous with global warming.
Evidence from the ice ages shows that the
carbon-dioxide greenhouse has always played a
crucial role in shaping the climate, but only as
one part of a symphony of effects which few people
pay attention to. Other factors may redistribute
extra heat in the atmosphere so as to leave
temperatures at ground 1evel unchanged. Spreading
high wispy clouds might reflect sunlight back into
space. Other mechanisms may need study, too, as
climatic theories evolve. New discoveries a1 ways
bring in their wake modish theories to explain
them.
The poli ticians who wi11 gather in Washington
for a meeting on climate change wil1 hear the
climatologists’ current estimates： a warming of
between 2℃ and 6℃ before 2100. They wi11 also
hear how utterly uncertain thoes estimates are. The
uncertainties wil1 not go away： political decisions
about global warming wil1 always be made on a
teetering balance of probabilities. If and when the
warming starts (i t is not clear that nay
greenhouse-caused warming has taken place so far)
its future rate and effect will remain in doubt.
Arguments about whether greenhouse warming is
al ready happening miss the point. 11 does not
matter whether this May’s darling buds are shaken
by greenhouse winds or ordinary ones. What matters

is whether future droughts will kil1 the trees they
bloom on.
People who seek to shape the climatic future
should bear in mind the past. This reveals that
climate change, one triggered, tends to gather a
momentum of its own. Falis in atmospheric carbon
dioxide -- smaller than the rises predicted for
this century and the next -- appear to set off ice
ages. Once carbondioxide levels are up, they stay
up for centuries. Another message from the past is
that even i f a “greenhouse world” in which many
places are warmer and damper may be attractive,
getting there will not be. Most environments do not
take kindly to sudden changes. Forests take time to
migrate, deserts do not bloom overnight. Even a
couple of degrees Celsius of warming in a century
would still be much quicker than anything since the
end of the most recent ice age. Rich countries may
be able to ride out such ecological upheavals. Poor
ones may not.
Such lessons from the past need to be mixed with
tomorrow’s uncertainties： it may never happen. For
now, the wisest course is to let the risk of global
warming act as an extra spur for doing only those
things that would be wise even if there were no
such risk. These include banning the ozone-chomping
CFCs. encouraging cleaner and more efficient
engines, saving tropical forests from the torch and
saw, exploring energy sources I ike the sun and the
wind, and improving nuclear power. To go beyond
such prudence is a large step, betokening the
beginning of a new endeavour： planet management.

The one-mi11enni um manager
Man has of ten changed nature -- wiping out a
species here, stripping a region of woodlands there
-- but in a piecemeal sort of way. Now people
wonder whether to wield the power that two
centuries of technology have given them and have a
shot at global air-conditioning. Waging war on
carbon dioxide by cutting down on the use of fossil
fuels would be only a first step. The climate
changes constantly, and once man thinks he has
seized the controls to avert some disastrous
man-made alteration, he wil1 be forever jiggling
them to steer his world through natural changes
that will fol low.
If today’s politicians worry about the
greenhouse effect, their successors the day after
tomorrow will have to worry about ice ages. The
next ice age is probably nearer in time than the
death of Julius Caesar, perhaps closer than the
coronation of Charlemagne. Such stretches of time
sond thankfully huge to politicians. But if they
start to play at planet management, they wil1 need
to learn to think in centuries.

1. It used to be said that facts speak for
themselves. This is, of course, untrue. The

it is he who decides to which facts to give the

2. The cost of the internal transportation system
in a big city is massive. Year by year the cost
of the oil and electricity consumed in the
hauling of people has been accumulating, and so
has the human cost, in physiological wear and
tear.

3. The responsibility for change, therefore, lies
with us. We must begin with ourselves, teaching
ourselves not to close our minds prematurely to
the novel, the surprising, the seemingly
radical. This means fighting off the
idea-assassins who rush forward to kill any new
suggestion on grounds of its impracticality,
while defending whatever now exists as
practical, no matter how absurd, oppressive, or
unworkable it may be. It means fighting for
freedom of expression -- the right of people to
voice their ideas, even if heretical.

4. Today the shops of Chinese cities are crammed
with goods and customers. The streets are lined
with billboards advertising the good life to an
audience held captive by traffic jams of
foreign-made cars. Foreign investors are
clamouring at the door.
All this is happening because Deng
Xiaoping’s reforms have unleashed an economic
revolution from the bottom up that China’s
rulers have concluded they must adapt to rather
than suppress. Chinese Communists have been
little better than their European counterparts
at running those bits of the economy under their
direct control.

5. Science has its architects and its buiiders -its theorists and its experimentalists. The
architects design abstract frameworks -- the
theory of natural selection, say, or the 火eneral
theory of relativity -- that purport to
accommodate large amounts of data. The builders
then gather those data, try to fit them within
the framework, and, in the process, subject the
designs to scientific evaluation. If the data
fit sol idly in pl ace, the design receives some
measure of vindication, and the buiiders seek
more material to complete the structure. If the
design is faulty to begin with, though, sooner
or later the entire theoretical edifice will
come crashing down, and it will be left for the
architect -- or, more often, for other
architects -- to formulate a framework that more
sturdily supports the data.

In analyzing factors Iikely to induce depression it is useful to distinguish between “life events”
and “life circumstances, ” both of which promote stress though in different ways. Stressful life events
include divorce or loss of a spouse and loss of employment. Stress-inducing “life conditions” include
single parenthood, low income, poor education, and responsibility for young children, circumstanes that
most often afflict the single-parent family head who is nearly always a woman. Any particular incident
of depression is likely to include elements from both categories.
As expected, epidemiological studies show that more women than men exhibit signs of depression. The
sex difference in rates of depression is also explained by a condition of 1earned helplessness. Society
encourages women to be passive, not aggressive； not to seek power, but to trust others and to nurture
others； to put the needs of others before their own； to appreciate mastery in others and not threaten
them with their own. So any particular incident of depression may include a past history of 1earned
helplessness as well as an immediate environmental agent of depression.

Q38. According to the passage, wind over the ocean
generally does which of the following?

—

The transfer of heat and water vapor from the
ocean to the air above it depends on a
disequilibrium at the interface of the water and
the air. Within about a millimeter of the water,
air temperature is close to that of the surface
water, and the air is nearly saturated with water
vapor. But the differences, however small, are
crucial, and the disequilibrium is maintained by
air near the surface mixing with air higher up,
which is typically appreciably cooler and lower in
water-vapor content. The air is mixed by means of
turbulence that depends on the wind for its energy.
As wind speed increases, so does turbulence, and
thus the rate of heat and moisture transfer.
Detai led understanding of this phenomenon awaits
further study. An interacting -- and complieating
-- phenomenon is wind-to-water transfer of momentum
that occurs when waves are formed. When the wind
makes waves, it transfers important amounts of
energy -- energy that is therefore not available to
provide turbulence.

similarities in the various ways in which the

2. One of the most important steps ever taken by
primitive man in his unconscious efforts to
escape from barbarism was the discovery of the
wheel. It took man a long time to discover that
rolling produced less friction than sliding, and
even then he had no idea of the mechanical
principle involved. Nor was the discoverer urged
on by visions of luxury and ease.

3. Has the U.S. too grown sclerotic? Perhaps, but
don’t count on it. Not this week anyway. The
genius of democracy is that about twice a decade
it produces a new President. Political equations
can be rewritten. Policies can be reversed.
Structures can be remade. Will that happen this
time? We don’t know yet. But the American
blessing is to have invented a system that
reopens that question -- and allows us to
reimagine the world -- every four years.

4. Today natural science and philosophy certainly
seem to be moving in different directions, and
it is commonly said that this journeying on
separate roads is only the outcome of the
increasing attention to special narrow fields of
learning, which the great growth of detailed
knowledge has made necessary. If the present-day
scientist has to go through the mass of material
put together by earlier experts and the theories
produced by them, before he had any hope of
being able to put his brick on to the structure
of science, how is he to have the time to get
all the knowledge and training of the man whose
business is philosophy?

5. The task of the philosopher of art is more
fundamental than that of the art critic in that
the critic’s pronouncements presuppose answers
to the questions set by the philosopher of art.
The critic says that a given work of music is
expressive； but the philosopher of art asks what
is meant by saying that a work of art is
expressive and how one determines whether it is.
In speaking and writing about art, the critic
presupposes that he is dealing with clear
concepts, the attainment of which is the task of
the philosopher of art.

One of these new ways is “recycling. ” Through recycling, usable materials are taken out of trash and
made into something else. These usable parts of trash are put through the cycle of going from a raw
material to a finished product again.
In some cities a machine cal led a Hydrapulper is being used to help recycle garbage. A Hydrapiilper is
like a huge mixing machine. The garbage is dumped onto a conveyor belt that feeds the machine. At the
same time, water is pumped into the Hydrapulper. (The machine got its name from hydra, which means
“water.”) With a swirling and mixing action, the Hydrapulper throws out the heavy metal objects that can
later be sold as scrap metal. The rest of the rubbish -- paper, food, plastic, rubber, rags, glass,
wood, leaves, and other items -- disintegrates. The rubbish is then mixed with water and carried in a
slush to another piece of equipment where glass, sand, and small pieces of metal are spun out.
At the end of the process, combustible organic materials are separated out and put into another
vessel. Here they are oxidized as they hit against grains of hot sand being blown around at high speed
in the vessel.
With the Hydrapulper, up to 95 percent of the original garbage is reclaimed or oxidized. The
remainder is turned into incinerator ash.

A. General Reading (Q1~Q4)

Extended debate concerning the exact point of origin of individual folktales told by Afro-American
slaves has unfortunately taken precedence over analysis of the tales’ meaning and function. Cultural
continuities with Africa were not dependent on importation and perpetuation of specific folktales in
their pristine form. It is in the place that tales occupied in the lives of the s1aves and in the
meaning slaves derived from them that the clearest resemblances to African tradition can be found.
Afro-American slaves did not borrow tales indiscriminately from the Whites among whom they lived. Black
people were most influenced by those Euro-American tales whose functional meaning and aesthetic appeal
had the greatest similarity to the tales with deep roots in their ancestral homeland. Regardless of
where slave tales came from, the essential point is that, with respect to language, delivery, details of
characterization, and plot, slaves quickly made them their own.

On May 8, 1939 folk song collector and scholar
Herbert Halpert arrived in Mississippi to document
folklore and folk music during a recording tour of
the South sponsored by the Joint Committee on the
Arts of the Works Progress Administration (WPA). He
drove into the state in an old ambulance outfitted
with cabinets, a small cot, food, and clothes. The
ambulance also had specially built shelves for the
latest in recording equipment -- an acetate disc
recorder lent by the Archive of American Folk Song
at the Library of Congress.
To take full advantage of Halpert’s short visit,
local WPA workers acted as intermediaries,
preceding the recording truck to make arrangements
with the folk musicians he would visit and grouping
artists in convenient places to minimize travel and
maximize recording time. Fol lowing their schedule,
with a few side trips to pursue a couple of leads
of his own, Halpert cut 168 records between May 8
and June 11, 1939. Abbott Ferriss, a Mississippi
native, assisted him.
In addition to helping with the actual
recording, Ferriss kept fieldnotes on the trip and
took photographs of the musicians, their families,
homes, and surroundings. At the project’s
conclusion the recordings became part of the
folk-music col lections at the Library of Congress.
The photographs and much of the manuscript material
related to the project remained in Mississippi.

“To Remember Me ... ”
Roloer^'t N. Tesrt
The day wi11 come when my body will lie upon a wiite sheet
neatly tucked under four corners of a mattress located in a hospital
busily occupied with the living and the dying.
At a certain moment a doctor wil1 determine that my brain has ceased to function
and, for all practical purposes, my life has stopped.
When that happens, do not attempt
to instill artificial life into my body
by the use of a machine.
And don’t call this my deathbed.
Let it be called the Bed of Life,
and let my body be taken from it
to help others lead fuller lives.
Give my sight to the man
who has never seen a sunrise,
a baby’s face or love in the eyes of a woman.
Give my heart to a person
whose own heart has caused nothing but endless days of pain.
Give my blood to a teenager
who was pul led from the wreckage of his car,
so that he might live to see his grandchiidren play.
Give my kindeys to one who depends on a machine to exist.
Take my bones, nerve and muscle in my body
and find a way to make a crippled child walk.
Explore every corner of my brain.
Take my cells, if necessary,
and let them grow so that, someday,
speechless boy will shout at the crack of a bat
a deaf girl will hear the sound of rain against window.
Burn what is left and scatter my ashes to the winds
to help the flowers grow.
If you must bury something,
let it be my faults, my weaknesses
and all prejudice against my fellow man.
Give my sins to the devil；
give my soul to God.
If, by chance, you wish to remember me,
do it with a kind deed or word
to someone who needs you.
If you do all I have asked,
I will live forever.

※ 다음 밑줄친 부분을 번역하시오.
1. Plato’s vision of the Republic was that poets
must be exiled lest they should lead men astray.
But was it not also Plato’s wisdom to complement
his reasoning with myths, which evidence man’s
poetic thinking? Surely Plato was a man who was
at odds with himself.

2. This public prominence of science has its effect
on scientists, too. For one thing, there are a
lot more scientists than there once were. For
another thing, the publicity and attention given
to science put the scientist in the 1imelight,
and many scientists are more cautious and less
radical in their work and thought than they
might otherwise be. This slows the advance of
science.

3. For their existence and comfort men depend on
certain products of the earth. These cannot be
used in common, however, without certain
disputes arising, nor do natural products
suffice unless they are improved by human labor.
Yet no one works unless he wil1 receive some
benefits to himslef. Therefore, certain rules
arise implying a mutual recognition of rights
and the institution of private property.
Briefly, such is a general utilitarian account
of the origin of the ideal of justice and of its
relation to human interests.

4. Anyone with nostalgia for the unchanging days of
the cold war might derive some pleasure from the
stony negotiations taking place between North
and South Korea, These two quite little
countries seemingly do their best to reproduce
the tension that existed worldwide when there
were two superpowers. Stalin’s ghost lives on in
the North, while the South claims to be the
defender of all that is good. An iron curtain
across the Korean peninsula divides them. Their
representatives usually meet in Panmunjom, a
border hamlet that serves as a humble, divided,
Berl in.

5. The great variety of taste, as well as of
opinion, which prevails in the world is too
obvious not to have fallen under everyone’s
observation. Men of the most confined knowledge

A. General Reading (QI^Q4)

Private enterprise is no stranger to the American prison. When the United States replaced corporal
punishment with confinement as the primary punishment for criminals in the early 19th century, the
private sector was the most frequent employer of convict labor. Prisoners were typically either leased
to private companies who set up shop in the prison or used by prison officials to produce finished goods
for a manufacturer who supplied the raw materials to the prison. The former arrangement was called the
contract system, while the latter came to be known as the piece-price system. In both instances, a
private company paid the prison a fee for the use of prison labor, which was used to partially offset
the expense of operating the prison. Blatant exploitation of inmates sometimes developed as a
consequence of these systems.
Opposition to the use of prison labor from rival manufacturers and from the growing organized labor
movement began to emerge in the latter part of the 19th century as more and more prisoners were put to
work for the private sector. Opposition reached a peak during the Great Depression when Congress passed
a series of laws designed to prohibit the movement of prison-made goods in interstate commerce, thus
insuring that these products would not compete with those made by outside labor. Many state legislatures
fol lowed suit, forbidding the open market sale or importation of prison-made goods within their borders
and effectively barring the private sector from the prison. As a consequence, prison-based manufacturing
operations became state-owned and operated businesses, selling goods in a highly restricted market.

In August 1980, according to a New York
Times/CBS news poll, 36 percent of the voters
called themseves Republican or said they were
independents leaning towards being Republicans. In
November 1984, the Republican fi gure rose to 47
percent. But in the latest Timers7cBs survey, the
Republicans were down to 38 percent. Therefore, the
Democrats are likely to win the next election.

Some political philosophers have observed that
conquest cannot serve as the stable base for the
possession and exercise of political power.
Rousseau said it： “The strongest man is never
strong enough to be always master unless he
transforms his power into right and obedience into
duty.”
Conquest is achieved by force and violence, by
armies wielding weapons, by invasion and
occupation, but the transformation of might into
right is achieved by persuasion, by persuasion of a
claim to legitimate rule.
In Afghanistan, we see that rulers may achieve
power by force, but that simple possession of power
does not obligate submission -- it may even
obligate resistance. The Afghan people -- invaded,
overrun, murdered, occupied -- resist. Their
resistance is a modern legend. Slated for
incorporation, absorption, secularization, the
Afghan people refuse to acquiesce in the
destruction of their society, culture, themselves
as a nation.

洪 다음을 읽고 물음에 답하시오. (Q37〜Q40)
Open government statutes in California have
proved both beneficial and harmful. In the energy
commission for example, as in other government
commissions, nearly all decisions must be made in
public session for which at least seven day’s
notice must be given. Which decisions can be made
by the executive director and which are strictly
reserved for the commission becomes quite important
in this context. If something is a matter for the
commission, there must be a public notice with
attendant publicity and preparation of materials
for distribution at the meeting. Furthermore, a
commissioner may not meet informally with another
commissioner nor with the executive di rector or any
member of his staff to discuss commission
activities. Such behavior would be a violation of
open government statutes. Staff briefings must take
place commissioner by commissioner or through a
commissioner’s advisors. More frequently,
commissioners or their advisors contact the staff
for information, but all such requests must be
submitted in writing.
An example of the impact of open government on
the operating procedures of a commission was
illustrated by the energy commission’s budgetary
process. The budget for the commission, unlike that
prepared in other state agencies, was prepared in
public session by the five commissioners. The
session was not simply a “review and comment”
session since the commissioners had not previously
discussed the budget. Every item proposed for the
budget could be commented upon by anyone who
attended the session.
Perhaps open government’s effect has been
greatest in the promulgation of rules and
regulations. Complaints have arisen from several
legislators and news media about the slowness of
the energy commission in setting regulations. If,
however, a commission attempts to handle fewer
matters without input from state agencies and
interested groups in open meetings, it will be
criticized for circumventing the open government
intentions. If present practices continue, the
commission wil1 continue to be criticized for
moving too slowly.

io > Recommendat i ons for Graduates
HOW YOU PLAY THE GAME OF LIEF

By WIN BORDEN, President of Minnesota Associat ion of commerce and Industry
Deliver cd to rhe St. Cloud State University Graduales, St. Cloud, M inncsot a, March 1, 1985
It was 20 years ago when I sat where you sit
this morning. As I thought about my remarks for
today, I tried to recall the essence of the
commencement address at my graduation. I can’t
remember a word that was said, or even who the
speaker was. It’s humbling to think my remarks may
leave such an indelible impression on your minds.
Deciding just what to say at a commencement
speech is difficult. Luckily, one of the few things
I’m good at is asking for advice. I need lots of
it. I asked my wife for a suggestion. She said,
“Well, there’s a first time for everything. Why
don’t you try to be funny.” I asked my 5-years-old
son how long I should talk. He said “Please Dad,
don’t talk for more than ten hours.” He likes short
speeches, but his time frame is not too precise.
His comment reminded me of the shortest
commencement speech in history. Clarence Darrow,
the famous Iawyer and orator, was asked to give his
advice to graduates at the time of the monkey
trial. The auditorium was packed. The introduction
was long and flowery. Darrow’s speech consisted of
one word repeated 3 times. “Survive, survive,
survive. ” That’s all he said and sat down.
The political satirist Art Buchwald gave another
short speech at a graduation ceremony at Georgetown
University. Let me repeat his entire speech.
“I’m here today to congratulate 987
graduating men and 856 graduating persons. I
have examined your grades. Your collective
entry into the world of business marks the
end of the free enterprise system as we know
it. Thank you. ”
Last week, as I was sitting down to put these
remarks together, I decided to pose a question to
several of the happiest and most successful people
I know. I chose a former congressman, a couple of

well known journalists and a number of business
leaders... and I asked them this' “Think back to
your college commencement speech. Give me either
the best piece of advice you received, or the best
piece of advice your speaker could have offered.”
Not surprisingly, no one remembered who spoke at
their commencement, or what, if any, relevant
advice was offered. But everyone had an opinion
about what they should have been told. So, in my
admittedly vain and probably futile effort to make
the first relevant graduation speech in the history
of academia, I’m going to pass along the
recommendations they made to me. Some you’ve
probably heard many times before. Some may surprise
you. Some you may disagree with.
First, in terms of your professional life, get
ready for some fun.
The working world is not just cold, dry
drudgery. Those of you who are Doonesbury fans may
remember a Sunday strip some years back in the days
when many col1ege students hated the thought of
moving into the business and professional world.
Zonker Harris and Mark Slackmeyer noticed a
despondent student coming out of the library.
Zonker asked, “What’s the problem?” The student
replied, “It’s nothing anybody can do anything
about. It’s just that tomorrow I’m graduating and
on Monday I’m assuming a position as a junior vice
president of the Chase Manhatten Bank of New York. ”
Zonker is immediately shocked and saddened and
says, “Hey man, I’m sorry, I didn’t know.” Well,
Zonker was a pessimist in those days, and
unnecessarily so. The point is simply that the
adventures you have, the success you achieve as you
take your place in your chosen profession, wil1
hopefully result in an enjoyment of 1ife which is
now difficult to imagaine. In other words, the good
times aren’t over. The really good times are, for
you, just beginning.

degrees, real estate promoters, local lawyers,
local clergymen.... The businessmen, who take up
the local traffic in merchandising, litigation,
church enterprise and the like, commonly begin with
some share in the real estate speculation. This
affords a common bond and a common ground of
pecuniary interest, which commonly masquerades
under the name of local patriotism, public spirit,
civic pride, and the like. This pretense of public
spirit is so consistently maintained that most of
these men come presently to believe in their own
professions on that head. Pecuniary interest in
local land values involves an interest in the
continued growth of the town. Hence any creditable
misrepresentation of the town’s volume of business
traffic, population, tributary farming community,
or natural resources, is rated as serviceable to
the common good. And any member of this
businesslike community wi11 be rated as meritorious
citizen in proportion as he is serviceable to this
joint pecuniary interest of these “influential
citizens. ”

The conviction that in after 1ife we must
struggle to remain thinking as freely and feeling
as deeply as we did in our youth has accompanied on
my road through life as a faithful adviser.
Instinctively, I have taken care not to become what
is generally understood by the term, a man of ripe
experience. The word “ripe” applied to persons
always did, and does sti11, convey to me the idea
of something depressing. What we are usually
invited to contemplate as “ripeness” in a man is
the resigning of ourselves to an almost exclusive
use of the reason. One acquired it by copying
others and getting rid, one by one, of the thoughts
and convictions which were dear in the days of
one’s youth. We believed once in the victory of
truth. We believed once in goodness. We trusted once
in the power of kindness and peaceableness. I
listened, in my youth, to conversations between
grown-up people. They 1ooked back at the idealism
and capacity for enthusiasm of their youth as
something precious which they ought to have held
fast, and yet at the same time they regarded it as
almost a law of nature that no one should be able
to do so. This woke in me a dread of having ever,
even once, to look back on my own past with such a
feeling. I resolved never to let myself become
subject to this tragic domination of mere reason,
and what I thus vowed in almost boyish defiance I
have tried to carry out.

In the previous time, the authors wrote
biographies by condensing an individual’s life, but
nowadays biographywriting is getting harder and
harder with the fact that only pieces and fragments
of an individual’s life are published, in which
condensation of a man’s life renders it
significant. Biography 1iterally means
life-writing, or the history of individual life. A
certain scholar once tried to write a woman’s
biography, but after the woman was married, she
took her husband’s name, and in this respect the
author was confronted with the problem of choosing
the right name for this situation. Specifically
there can be no true del ineation between
biographical and autobiographical writing unless
the author is one’s self. In fact, the woman should
use her original surname. If her maiden name is
Jones and she is married to John Smith, then her
name should be Jones in her biography. In writing
the contents, a writer should simplify important
synopsis. A piece should be garnered from the
overall content. Looking at autobiographies from a
literary rather than a historical point of view,
one can detect a number of variables. They differ,
first in the proportion of physical to mental
events； the space given to the things done and seen
and the persons known on the one hand, and to
the thoughts and emotions of the autobiographer on
the other： secondly, they differ in variety and
breadth, according to the opportunities and
experience of the author and the range of his
interests and ideas. Thirdly, there is a moral
variation with respect to certain related factors；
the activity and reliability of the
autobiographer’s memory, his honesty and balance,
and the candor of his disclosures and opinions.
Lastly, there are artistic differences with arise
from the varying ski 11 with which the author
selects the signi ficant, disposes the material,
appreciates the interrelation of cause and effect,
and evokes from the multiplicity of life a unifying
pattern.

theorized that atoms must be mainly empty space
with a small nueleus in the center. That being so,
electrons must orbit the nucleus； yet wouldn’t
charged electrons lose all their energy and fall
into the nucleus? In 1913 Niels Bohr proposed that
electrons behaved in quantum fashion. They remained
in fixed orbits and moved from one orbit to another
-- in quantum leaps -- when they emitted or
absorbed energy. The neutron, the atom’s last part
until accelerators revealed more, was found in 1932
by James Chadwick. Theorist and experimenter were
united in the person of Enrico Fermi, who studied
electrons and gases before buiiding the first
fission reactor that led to the atomic bomb and
nuclear power.

The mistletoe plant grows on deciduous trees -those that lose their leaves in autumn. It is
spread by birds as they eat its white berries and
then wipe their beaks on the bark, of nearby
branches. The sticky seeds put out tiny rootlets,
thrust up 1eaves, and begin an extremely long life.
Wintry ice and parching summers cause it no harm.
Virtually indestructible, it dies only when the
tree dies. For the tree, it is only a minor pest,
manufacturing its own food from the chlorophyl of
its leaves and using the tree simply as a source of
liquid and vital minerals.

Cultural barriers would not be important if the
various groupings of people on this planet never
came into contact with one another. There would be
no need to communicate with people who speak a
different language and who conduct their lives
according to a different set of assumptions about
the many aspects of existence. But it is precisely
because the world is not made up of isolated groups
of people that cultural barriers are so important.
The fact is, as Marshal 1 McLuhan and others have
pointed out, that the enormous increase in
population and the great advances in mass
communication
and
transportation that have occurred
over the past century and a half have brought about
a greater intermixing of peoples and cultures than
these
ever before. The continuation of
developments, together with the rapidly increasing
economic interdependence among nations, would seem
to guarantee even more widespread and increasingly
frequent cultural intermixing in the future as the
multiplicity of societies evolves towards the
“global village” McLuhan speaks of. The prospect
before us is that relatively few individuals, and
even fewer of the world’s cultunes, wi11 escape
being touched in some way by the intercultural
experience.

The mother mantis normally abandons her egg mass
and therefore never sees or cares for her numerous
progeny. Marauding ants carry off many mantes as
they are born. But once free and active, the
spindly babies disperse at once, escaping the
instantly mani fested predatory instincts of their
siblings.
The pale, black-eyed mini-mantis at first can
eat only tiny insects such as aphides, but as they
grow during a sequence of skin sheddings they take
on larger prey. Over the weeks, however, few of
the original clutch survive environmental hazards.
After its final molt, a mantis grows mature and,
in most species, fully winged. Now the leggy insect
is ready to search for prey, mate, lay eggs, and
repeat the ageless reproductive cycle.

The value of philosophy lies largely in its very

beliefs of his age or his national, and from

The dilation or contraction of the
chromatophores is effected by muscular radial
processes, which connect the color cells with the
surrounding skin musculature, and these processes
in turn are innervated by nerves communication with
the brain. It appears that impulses sent from the
central nervous system to the chromatophores are
responsible for all the color changes, though there
may be simple pulsations of the chromatophores
unconnected with the central nervous system.
Furthermore, there is a remarkably delicate
adjustment in cephalopods between the eye and the
chromatopohores； that is to say, the change of
color in an animal to correspond with its
background depends solely upon the excitation of a
reflex which passes from the retina through the
optic nerve to the brain and thence by the various
nerve trunks to the chromatophores. It has been
shown that the degree of rapidity with which an
octopus or squid can change color and the degree of
bri1liancy of the colors he assumes are
commensurate with the degree of development of his
eye.
Color changes apparently respond also to the
cephalopod’s emotions； he seems to blanch when
frightened and flush a dark color when angered, and
such chances are powerful enough to overrule his
natural impulse to assume a color which simulates
his background and changes with it.

The body temperature of cold-blooded animals
such as fish, frogs, and snakes goes up and down
depending on the outside temperature. Warm-blooded
animals keep more or less the same temperature
within their bodies. But even warm-blooded animals
must find a way of protecting themselves against
sudden and sharp temperature changes. One good way
to survive under such hardship is to live
underground. At about 1-1/2 feet below the surface,
it is cooler in summer and warmer in winter. And
so the desert animals, rodents chiefly, live
underground -- especially in daytime. Typical of
these below-ground rodents is the prairie dog,
found in North America, and Alpine pika of the
Mongolian steppes in Asia.

Al though a jet engine and a rocket engine
operate on the principle of Newton’s Third Law,
they differ in that a jet must take in oxygen from
the air to burn its fuel, but a rocket must carry
its own oxygen. Gases escaping under great pressure
in one direction exert a push on the engine in the
opposite direction. According to Newton’s Third
Law, to each action there is an equal and opposite
reaction. You can illustrate the principle by
blowing up a rubber balloon moves forward as the
air escapes in the opposite direction.

===== PAGE 601 =====
GRADUATE ENGLISH

A GUIDELINE FOR USERS
“A man of two languages is worth two men." — Rev. Y. H. Kim

잉＞ DIY = Do It Yourself! 싸
다음은 GRADUATE ENCASH Wlume 2. NOTEBOOK(해설서)의 사용자를 위한 ‘일러두기’이다.

NOTEBOOK은 철저하게 Wlume 1. WORKBOOK을 토대로 한 것인 만큼 학습자는 WORKBOOK의 Guideline올 먼저 읽은 뒤
다음을 참고하는 것이 바람직하다.

NOTEBOOK

의 수록 범위

- Volume 1. WORKBOOK의 핵심을 이루는
• 제1강 ~ 제10강의 本講 전체와
• 보충강좌 중 Antonym Test 20회분 및
• 권말 Final Test 12회분을, WORKBOOK과 같은 분량인 총 600페이지의 지면에 망라해 놓았다.
- 따라서 WORKBOOK 에서 빠진 부분은 이미 그 자체가 해설 방식으로 제시되어 있거나 해설의 실익이 별로 없는 제 1 부 지상강좌 전체와
제 3 부 보충강좌 중 Accent, Pronunciation, Spelling 및 Composition Test 뿐인데, 해설 중 이 부분을 참고하도록 = 기호로 연결해 놓
은 경우가 있으므로, 필요시 수시로 열람해야 한다.

NOTEBOOK

Y

이 표방하는 정신: 미

- DIY 란 do-it-yourself 의 약어 (abbreviation) 로, 사전적인 뜻은 ‘the practice of doing repairs, painting house, etc. oneself’, 즉 ‘손수
꾸미기, 직접하기’의 의미이다.

- WORKBOOK 을 집필하면서 가장 큰 고민은 어떻게 하면 학습자가 문법 • 어휘 • 독해를 분리시키지 않고 종합적으로 학습하도록 유기적
으로 결합시키느냐였고, 그것도 남의 도움을 빌지 않고 스스로 연구하고, 필요하다면 누구에게 배우기에 앞서 동료학습자와 토론을 할 수
있도록 동기부여를 할 수 있을까 하는 것이었다. 여기에는 시중에 범람하는 영어참고서들이 천편일률적으로 학습자를 수동적인 학습자세
에 젖게 만드는 소위 ‘떠먹이기식’의 편제와 ‘주입식’위주의 영어강의 일변도에 대한 필자의 강한 불만이 내재되어 있었다. 결과적으로는
필 자 의 취 지 가 상 당 히 실 효 를 거 두 고 있 어 더 할 나 위 없 이 기 쁜 데 , 상 위 권 의 학 습 자 도 평 균 50~60% 를 상회하지 못하는 GRADUATE

ENGLISH 전편에 걸친 난이도의 영향 탓인지는 모르겠으나, 아무튼 GRADUATE ENGLISH 의 독자 만큼은 누구보다도 사전을 찾는 습
관과 스스로 연구하는 요령올 익히고 있고, 여기저기서 GRADUATE ENGLISH 를 들고 앉아 삼삼오오 토론하는 분위기가 조성되고 있
기 때문이다.
- 그 러 나 영 어 학 습 에 만 전 력 투 구 를 할 수 없 는 고 시 준 비 생 들 과 같 은 독 자 들로부터 계속되는 독촉과 해설서 발간 시기를 묻는 문의가 쇄도
하는 와중에서 NOTEBOOK!- 집필하면서 필자가 씨름한 고민 아닌 고민은, 어떻게 하면 WORKBOOK 의 DIY 효과를 NOTEBOOK 에
서 퇴색시키지 않느냐에 있었다. 왜냐하면 기실 해설서라는 것은 그 속성상 학습자가 스스로 해야할 것을 대리로 (by proxy) 충분히 챙겨
주는 것이므로, 그러면서도 학습자가 스스로 연구하고 나아가 동료들과 토론하도록 유도한다는 것은, 이미 그런 기대 자체가 irony 가 아닐
수 없기 때문이다.
- 해서, NOTEBOOK 에서는 충분한 해설을 해 주면서도, 시간［특히, 사전찾는 시간］은 덜어 줄지언정, 스스로 학습하는 이상의 노력을 쏟게
하여 소기 이상의 성과를 거두게끔 학습자와 저자 사이에 눈에 보이지 않는 공방전(?)을 펼치고 있다. 예컨대,
• 애초 해설서를 별권으로 기획한 것에서부터,
• 해설을 해 주면서도 스스로 최종 결정을 내릴 수 있는 소지를 남겨 두거나,
• 충분한 이해를 위해서는 잠시잠시 독자적으로 사고(思考)하도록 배려한 것이랄지,
• 때로는 엄청난 양의 학습자료를 제시하거나,
• 그리 어렵지 않은 예문의 음미는 독자에게 맡긴 것,
• 프 기호로 관련사항을 종횡무진 연결해 놓은 것 등,
학습자가 책장을 넘기는 속도의 완급을 조절하기 위해 최선을 다했다.

- NOTEBOOK 이 표방하는 DIY 정신의 백미( 白®) 는 Vocabulary Tip 과 더불어 각 강 말미의 SUB-NOTE 인데, SUB-NOTE 는 그 강에
서 학습한 내용 중 논란의 소지가 많은 항목 중 일부를 별도로［추가로(아］ 떼내어 독자와 문답식으로 토론하는 방식을 택했다.
- 이 모든 노력이 학습자가 ‘홀로서기’를 기대하는 善意 (goodwill) 에서 비롯된 것으로, 학습자에게 괴로움올 주려는 마음은 조금도 없는 만
큼, 독자 제위께서는 주어진 모든 자료를 인내를 가지고 충분히 학습함은 물론이요, 아무리 귀찮더라도 ［그렇지는 않고, 오히려 재미있을

• 강의와 집필이라는 토끼 두 마리를 쫓느라 고전분투하던 저자를 지원하기 위해 원고배달은 물론 홍보를 위해 동분서주 뛰어 주
신 과장님들 이하 전 부원과 양은정 실장 이하 사무직원들의 협조는 뜨거운 것이었다.
• 정원근 총무님께는 어떤 감사의 말씀을 드려야 할지 모르겠다. 독실한 신앙을 몸으로 실천하고 계시는 이 분은 이제는 형없는
저자에게 맏형 이상의 인연으로 자리잡고 있다. GRADUATE ENGLISH의 산뜻한 표지도안과 색상선택은 이 분의 작품이다.
- 이 모든 감사를 드리면서 저자가 기뻐할 수 있는 것은 모두 전기석 사장님의 덕택이다. WORKBOOK과 NOTEBOOK의 집필기간
동안 두 번씩이나 연구실을 마련해 주시어 저자는 모든 것을 잊고 冊에만 전념할 수 있었다. 평생올 출판업에 종사하시면서 모든
것을 겪으시고 이제는 대학가 일반영어 학습서 분야에서는 원로의 위치에 계신 이 분이 엄청난 초기비용의 위험부담에도 나 같은
«生에게 집필의 기회를 주신 것은 여간한 경영철학이 아니고서는 힘들었으리라. 돌이켜보니, 저자의 쓸데없는 아집이 善意의 사
장님께 불편을 드렸던 일이 있었는데, 이 자리를 통해 사과드린다.
- Last but not least, 늘 그림자처럼 옆에 있으면서 망둥이마냥 뛰어다니는 사내를 보필해온 내 아내...
우리 두 사람의 10년 숙원이던 2세를 뱃속에 안고서 만삭의 와중에도 하루 두 끼씩의 도시락 반찬을 꼬박꼬박 챙겨 준 그녀와
곧 태어날 아가에게 이 책을 바친다.

& EPILOGUE （ 터져 나오는 말）
-

-

-

일을 벌려놓는 것은 마무리하는 과정에 비하면 정말 아무 것도 아니라는 생각이 든다. 인생의 황금기를 앞날이 어찌될지 모르는
책 한 권（아니, 두 권）에 매달려 만 삼 년을 꼬박 보낸다. 고시공부를 해도 이 만큼 철저하게 할 수는 없었으리라. 그 삼 년 속에
평생을 압축해 놓은 회로애락과 영고성쇠가 반복되었다.
이렇게 과정을 합리화하고 아전인수격으로 읊조린들 무삼 소용이람? 독자 개개인의 지성과 가슴에 울려퍼지는 메아리가 없다면…
두 권의 쌍동이 같은 冊을 펼쳐 보이면서 부끄러움이 앞선다. 노력 외에는, 노력 외에는, 주장하는 바가 무엇이냐는 자책도 있다.
군데군데 꿰맨 상처들이 아픔으로 다가온다.
하루에도 몇 번씩 파김치처럼 늘어지려던 나를 붙들어 준 인연들이 고맙다. 이 책의 가능성을 안팎에 보여준 민족 高大人들의 호
옹이 고맙다. 일개 書生의 능력의 한계를 시간 말미를 허용해 가면서 끝까지 기다려 준 출판사의 인내가 고맙다. 불과 1년만에 나
보다 훌륭하신 여러 선•후배 선생님들이 이 책에 관심을 가지고 강의에 참여하시겠다는 의지를 보이시는 것은 대단히 고무적이다.
그 분들의 지적과 비판을 모두 겸허히 받아들이련다.
문득, WORKBOOK의 집필이 절정이던 어느 초겨울날, 삼국지의 장비처럼 까칠한 수염을 달고서 올라탄 택시에서 기사님이 저자
에게 들려주던 이야기가 생각난다. 민주주의는 가진 자가 없는 이에게, 쥔 자가 약한 이에게, 배운 자가 배우는 이에게 나누어주는
것이 아니냐는 말씀이었다. 이 책의 성격을 뒷받침해 주고, 나아가 이 넓은 세상에서 내가 할 일에 의미를 부여해 준 귀중한 일화

이다. 이제, 얼마 안 되는 것이나마 나누어 주어야겠다. 그러기 위해 더 공부해야겠다.
- 그리고, 이제 정말로 스스로에게 다짐컨대, 제발 좀 여유를 가지고 살아가야겠다. 옆도 보고 뒤도 보고 아래도 보면서... 때로는 다
리도 쭉 뻗어 가면서… 때로는 아무 생각없이 바보처럼 히히 웃어가면서...
- 그런데, 걱정이 하나 있다. 제 버룻 개 못 준다던데...

대부분의 아시아 국가들은 쌀이 주된 식용작물이다. 재배가 증가했
지만 증가하는 인구의 수요를 간신히 메워 왔올 뿐이다. 필리핀은 식
량생산이 인구 규모보다 약간 빠르게 증가했지만 1 인당 식량 수요의
휠씬 더 빠른 중가로 인해 새로운 부족이 생겼다. 한때 주요 쌀 수출
국이었던 인도네시아는 수년째 수입쌀에 의존하고 있다. 대부분 국가
가 현재의 필요를 간신히 메꾸고 있을 뿐으로, 큰 부족이 예상된다.
이들 국가에서 요구되는 농업 생산의 강화는 여타 자원에 잠재적
으로 불리한 부작용을 안고 있다. 텅빈 저수지의 훼손 효과는 자명하
다. 다른 문제점으로는 침수와 토양침식, 해충의 중가, 농경의 오염이
포함된다.

면 반드시 개발되어야 할 것으로 과학이 나타내 주는 단일 세계의

하는 것이 꽤 들어 있기 때문이다.)

제2 강 동사형 OVERVIEW 82

OVERVIEW

제2강동사형

기본 5형식은 개념이 단순하고 명쾌하여 구문을 쉽게 파악할 수 있다는 점에서 특히 학교 문법에서 기여하는 바가
크다. 이러한 장점에도 불구하고 5형식 만으로는 문형에 대한 고급 학습자의 호기심을 충족시키지 못한다. 그 이유는 첫
째 , 필수요소로 작용하는 부사어구 (Adverbial) 롤 간과하고 둘째, 구동사 (Phrasal Verts) 의 처리가 애매하며 셋째, 복잡할
수 있는 목적어, 보어의 하위분류(Sub-Classification)롤 무시하고, 넷째, 동사에 옷지 않게 유형을 세분화할 수 있는 형
용사형 (Adjective Patterns) 에 대해 언급조차 없기 때문이다. GRADUATE ENGLISH 에서는 동사형 (Verb Patterns) 과 관련하
여 기본 5형식을 수용하면서도 30개의 동사형으로 재분류하여 학습자가 각종의 시험에 대비하여 빈출 개별동사의 문형
에 항상 관심을 갖도록 문법• 어휘 •독해의 전편에 걸쳐 연계시켜 놓았다. 개별동사의 통사상 특성이 고급의 시험은 물론
일반 영어 전반에서 차지하는 비중은 아무리 강조해도 지나치지 않으며, 아울러 동사의미의 유사성 및 관련성으로 인해
문형을 착각할 소지가 있는 기본 동사들이 자주 출제됨에 유의해야 한다.

사실과 이론의 구분은 M. Comte와 그의 제자들이 중요하게 여겨
온 한 가지 주요 원칙을 낳는다. 그들은 현대 귀납적 연구의 우월성
이 바로 증명의 사용과 가능성에 있으며, 고대인들이 그들이 과학에
서 별로 진전을 이루지 못한 이유는 다름아닌 그들의 이론을 증명하
지 않았거나 또는 중명할 수 없었기 때문이라고 말한다. 중명이 과학
방법의 완전함을 위해 필수적이라는 것은 논란의 여지가 없다. 그러
나 철학적 연구의 많은 부문에서 무엇이 중명인가에 관해서는 여전
히 토론의 여지가 있다. 방법에 대한 철학이 인간 지식의 일차적인
근원에 대한 완벽한 목록을 주지 못하고 무엇이 일차적 진실의 원류
인지 혹은 관찰의 진실인지를 엄연히 결정하지 못하는 한 무엇이 정
당한 관찰에의 호소인지[관찰을 필요로 하는 것인지] 또는 무엇이 진
정한 증명인지 하는 문제는 계속 모호한 상태가 될 것이다.

우주에서의 무기사용 금지에 대한 빈번한 요청을 하면서도 소련
은 우주를 군사계획의 핵심으로 만들었다. 19 기년 이후로 소련은 미
국의 정찰위성올 파괴시킬 수 있는 세상에서 유일한 위성 파괴용 위
성을 보유해 왔다. 소련의 우주무기 금지제안은 이 새로운 전략적 고
지(高地)에서 미국올 군사적으로 열둥한 위치에 동결시키려는 냉소적
인 노력이다.

淡 다음을 읽고 물음에 답하시오. (34~36)
미국인들이 믿는 것과 그들이 사는 방식 사이의 관계를 이해함에 있
어서 이상과 현실을 구별하는 것이 중요하다. 기회의 균둥, 자립과 같은
미국인의 가치 기준이 꼭 미국인의 삶의 현실을 묘사하는 이상은 아니
다. 예를 들어, 기회의 균둥은 항상 실행되는 이상은 아니다. 실제로는
어떤 사람들은 다른 사람들보다 더 좋은 성공의 기회를 갖는다. 부유한
가정에 태어난 사람들은 가난한 가정에 태어난 사람들보다 더 많은기
회를 갖는다. 돈의 상속은 개인에게 결정적인 잇점을 안겨 준다. 모든
인종에 대해 기회의 균등을 촉진하려고 제정된 법이 있음에도 불구하고
많은 미국 흑인들은 평범한 미국 백인보다 기회가 적다.
미국의 이상이 실제 생활에서 단지 부분적으로 실행된다는 사실
이 그 이상의 중요성올 떨구지는 않는다. 대부분의 미국인들은 여전
히 미국의 이상을 믿고 있으며, 일상 생활에서 그 이상에 의해 크게
영향을 받는다. 만약 이러한 기본적인 미국의 가치 기준이 무엇인지,
그리고 어떤 면에서 그 가치 기준이 미국에서 거의 모든 생활의 국
면에 영향을 미치는지 이해할 수 있다면, 미국인들이 무엇을 생각하
고 느끼는지를 이해하는 것은 더 쉽다.

라는 것올 알고 있다는 데에 있다.

32. 다음 증거 중 고고학자들의 가설을 가장 잘 반박하는 것은?
(a) 1980년에 유골 10구가 발견됐다.
(b) 그 로마 해변은 만에서 500야드 떨어진 곳에 있다.
(c) 1709년에 한 갱부가 그 도시까지 굴을 뚫었다.
(d) 주택과 건물들이 그곳에 4000명 이상이 살았다는 것을 시사한다.
(e) 1982 년에 5 주간에 걸쳐 26구의 온전한 유골이 테라스 아래에 있
는 방들과 해변에서 발견되었다.
셰치 근거 (evidence) 가 충분할수록 논박 (refute) 에 유리하다. (a) 는
출처도 모르는 열 구의 유골만으로는 중거가 빈약하고, (b) 의 거리
가 멀다는 것도 대피를 반박할 수 있는 논리적인 근거로 미약하다.
(e) 의 짧은 기간 (5 주) 동안에 26 구의 유골을 도피하지 못한 실내나
더이상 도피할 곳이 없는 해안에서 찾았다는 것은, 더 발굴될 가능
성까지 감안한다면 답항 중 가장 확실한 근거가 될 수 있다.

Q: 여러 사전을 뒤져봐도 물고기를 주어로 be spawned라는 수동이 성
립하는 예운이 없습니다. 그냥 자동사로 spawns라고 하는 것이 맞지
않을까요?

A: spawn(알을 낳다)은 자•타동사 모두 가능하다. 여러 사전에서 자
동사의 예는 찾을 수 있지만 (예: The salmon fight their way
back up the river to spawn. - Collins Die.) 유감스럽게도
학습자의 지적처럼 be spawned는 보이지 않는다, 그러나 언어
에는 소위 생성적 특성(productive feature)이라는 것이 있어 다
른 표현을 흉내내는 경우가 있는데, 사전이 이 모든 것을 밝혀주
지는 못한다. 물론r알은 강에서 낳고, 생활은 바다에서 한다J는
문장도 쓸 수 있지만r강에서 태어나, 바다에서 산다」는 해석도
틀린 바가 없고, 따라서 주어진 문장의 be spawned는 be born
(as eggs)의 의미로 생성된 것으로 보면 된다. 문법적으로 be
spawned가 안 된다고 말할 수도 없자 않은가? 중요한 것은 문
법문제도 원문취지 파악이 선행되어야 한다는 것이며, 이런 문제
를 통해 살아 숨쉬는 언어의 다양한 특성을 이해하는 것이 바람
직하다.

Q: 답항 (a)와 (b)는 in 1906이 and 앞에 오느냐 뒤에 오느냐의 차이일
뿐으로 어느 쪽이든 나름대로 말이 되는데, 굳이 답을 (a)로 제시한
근거는 무엇입니까?

A: 근거는 불충분하다. 학습자의 이해를 돕기 위해 출전을 밝히면
GMAT의 Writing Ability Test의 item인데, 그 특유의 출제유
형 중 하나이다. Writing Ability라는 Section은 책자에 따라서
Sentence Correction이라고도 불린다. 개중에는 원문의 밑줄 친
부분에 하자가 없고 특별한 개선이 필요한 경우가 아니면 원문취
지를 바꾸지 말 것을 요구하는 문제가 더러 있다. 필자는 이런 문
제가 Native Speaker에게는 얼마나 중요한지 모르지만, 외국인
학습자의 경우 GMAT를 치르는 사람이 아니라면 언어능력 향상
과는 별개의 점수 따는 방법과 관련된 것이기에 당초부터
GRADUATE ENGLISH에 넣지 않기로 했다. 이 문제는 그저
시제의 일관성을 묻는 문제로 분류했던 것이다.
내친 김에, 독자 제위께서는 유치한 TOEFL, GRE, GMAT
둥속에 너무 현혹되지 말라. 필자는 시중에 범람하는 교재 중 전
면복제, 표절 둥 지극히 비양심적인 것들도 많이 보는데, 특히 속
이 얄팍한 Yankee들의 자칭 실용주의적 지침서에 나오는 몇 안
되는 GRE, GMAT 대비 요령을 제것인양 번역하여 살을 붙이고
는 ‘내 이론이요’하는 非영어전공자들도 있다. 차라리 원문 그대로
두면 어련히 대학생들이 알아서 할까? 각설하고, 위 문제유형에
대비하여 주의를 촉구하는 외국의 지침서를 인용해 드리니, 독자
제위께서는 이 천기를 누설하지 말라.

강 준동사 종합

준동사 (Verbals) 는 부정사•동명사•분사의 총칭이다. 준동사는 술어동사와 달리 12 시제나 주어의 인칭•수에 따라 변화하
지 않고, 文中에서 문법적 기능이나 다른 품사의 기능을 보인다. 술어동사로 쓰이지 않지만, 별도의 옥적어•보어•수식어롤
거느릴 수 있으며, 단순형을 기준으로 완료형과 수동형의 변형을 가진다. 필요시 의미상 주어를 취할 수 있고 not, never 의
부정어는 준동사 앞에 둔다.
학습자는 특히 스타일과 관련하여, 준동사가 문두에 부사적으로 제시될 때 준동사의 의미상 주어를 文의 주어와 일치
시켜 현수구문(Dangling Construction)을 피해야 한다.

침체되고 있는 미국 경제는 전 세계에 파장을 미친다. 미국인들은
콜롬비아산 커피로부터 일제 사진기에 이르기까지 모든 물품에 대해
세계 최대의 소비자이기 때문에, 미국 구매의 부진은 다른 국가들의
재정수입에 깊이 상처를 준다. 이러한 사실은 빈곤한 제3 세계 국가에
게는 더 많은 고충올, 그리고 부유한 미국 무역상대국들에게는 보다
둔화된 성장올 의미하는 것이다.

1. 윗글에 따르면?
(a) 침체된 미국경제는 막대한 소비의 결과이다.
(b) 미국 경제의 침체는 다른 많은 국가에 영향을 미칠 것이다.
(c) 미국인들은 콜롬비아산 커피와 일본산 사진기에 돈올 너무 많이
쓴다.
(d) 제3세계 국가와 부유한 미국 무역상대국들이 침체되고 있는 미국
경제에 대한 책임이 있다.

Rousseau는 자연상태의 인간은 동료인간과 다른 생물에 대한 동
정심으로 특징지어진다고 여겼다. 인간이 인간을 착취하는 것과 같은
사회악의 존재를 설명하기 위해, Rousseau는 우리 인간의 타고난 감
정이 매정한 사회제도의 중압올 받고 짓눌린다고 주장했다.
4. 위에 설명된 Rousseau의 논거는 어떻게 한지를 설명할 수
있다면 가장 잘 강화될 것인가?
(a) 현대사회로부터 자연상태로의 복귀가 될 수 있다.
(b) 사회제도가 우리의 타고난 동정심을 서로를 위해 길러줄 수 있도
록 우리가 사회제도를 재구성할 수 있다.

(c) 현대의 개혁론자들이 자연상태라는 이상에 어긋나지 않는 삶으로
길을 이끌어 갈 것이다.

(d) 모든 생물체에 대한 동정심의 특징을 본래부터 가지는 생물이 비
정한 사회제도를 만들어 낼 수 있었다.

각 언어의 배경이 되는 언어학적 체계(즉, 문법)는 단지 생각올
표현하기 위한 재생 도구가 아니라 그 자체가 사상을 형성시키는 것
이며, 개인의 정신활동, 인상의 분석, 정신적 도구의 합성을 위한 프
로그램이자 길잡이이다. 사상의 형성은 독립된 과정, 즉 구식발상에
서 말하는 이성적인 과정이 아니라, 특정한 문법의 일부분이며, 서로
다른 문법사이에서처럼 적게 혹은 크게 다양하다. 우리는 우리의 모
국어가 그어 놓은 선을 따라 자연을 구획한다. 우리가 현상계로부터
떼어 놓은 범주와 유형들은, 그 범주와 유형들이 모든 관찰자들을 정
면으로 쳐다보기 때문에 그곳(현상계)에서 013발견되는 것은 아니다.
한편, 그와는 반대로, 세상은 우리의 정신에 의해 — 그리고 이것은
주로 우리 정신 속에 있는 언어체계에 의한다는 것을 의미한다 —
형성되어야 하는 인상들의 만화경 같은 흐름 속에 나타난다. 우리는
자연을 나누고, 개념 속으로 자연을 조직화하고, 또한 우리가 실제로
행하는 바처럼 의미를 부여하는데, 그 주된 이유는 우리가 이러한 방
식으로 자연을 구성하기로 한 Q14 협약의 당사자들이기 때문이다. 이
협약은 우리의 언어 공동체 전역에서 유효하며 우리의 언어 유형 속
에 그 규칙이 마련되어 있다. 물론 이 협약은 암묵적이고 상술되지
않은 것이지만, 그 협약의 조건은 절대적으로 의무적인 것이다. 우리
는 그 협약이 포고한 정보의 구성과 분류에 의존하지 않고서는 한마
디도 할 수 없다.
